entries.title: Dystopian Sci Fi Books, recommended by Adrian Tchaikovsky
entries.summary: Sci fi dystopias are often, paradoxically, hopeful: they show oppressive systems, but they also show resistance. Award-winning author Adrian Tchaikovsky picks out five titles that deserve more readers, ranging from near-futures to space operas, but all featuring complex humans responding to dire circumstances. This interview appeared first on Five Books.
entries.content:
In our stressful world, why are we drawn to reading dystopias?

I think the appeal of dystopia is twofold. Firstly, as a reader and a writer, it’s very narratively fertile. In a dystopia, it is very clear what is wrong, which can go a variety of ways; and it is frequently a human-created wrong. So it gives you lots of fun friction points. You can explore the people who are genuinely having a dystopic time of it, and the people for whom that dystopia is a utopia – which of course is usually the case for someone.

What guided your choices today?

It was a very interesting exercise to think, ‘What is a dystopia?’ A lot of the things that came to mind were post-apocalypse stories, and I realised that a post-apocalypse world is not necessarily a dystopia. Post-collapse stories are not dystopian stories, because a dystopia has got to be in place and ingrained. You need a system that is actively oppressing, and has the stability and authority to oppress. So a lot of collapse stories, where the problem is that everything is falling apart, are not dystopias.

I was thinking about things like the Adam Robertson and Dave Hutchinson Aftermath series, which starts with Shelter. That’s a post-apocalypse story, but it’s not a dystopia story, because people are building up. Similarly, Claire North’s Notes From The Burning Age was another one I considered, but the hardships are not part of a system – they are part of a less caring environment, which I feel detracts from the core idea of dystopias. In a dystopia, the problem system is here to stay. It’s not a thing you build out of. It’s a thing you resist.

With this set, I’ve tried to give a variety of different takes. With one exception, they are relatively near-future – there’s one also that’s full-on wacky space opera dystopia. But they’re all flagging up different elements of what can go into a dystopian setting.

I’ve avoided anything that seemed too obvious. So, for example, The Hunger Games is an excellent dystopia series, but it’s also enormously well known. I feel that most people are going to discover that one on their own, probably through the film. And I have not put 1984 on this list, for example. I absolutely assume that people are going to come to 1984 on their own.

Then let’s talk about some books that deserve to be discovered. Starting with a Nebula and Hugo winner: Paolo Bacigalupi’s The Windup Girl. Tell us about this one.

This is a book I encountered when it was doing the rounds the first time, and yes, it did extraordinarily well, and deservingly so. It is set in a near-ish future, post an energy and climate collapse. It’s set in Thailand. The windup girl of the title is, to be blunt, essentially a sex-bot who is wandering around feral through a lot of the story. It’s not really about her – or it – that’s just an extra interesting thing that Bacigalupi is looking at.

There is a dystopian regime running Thailand, and the whole world is in a fairly poor situation. This book gives you the cold equations of what happens if you’re trying to run a state after the collapse of globalism: what it comes down to is calories. You don’t have fossil fuels – what fossil fuels you do have are very carefully hoarded – so all of your physical power is coming out of animal and human labour. Obviously that then takes calories. So how many calories does your wage buy you? How many calories are you exerting?

It is a grim and astonishingly well-realised picture of desperate people who have been left over in this crash of globalism. The regime is not a nice regime, but you can also have quite a lot of sympathy for the fact that they are having to make a lot of very tough decisions in the wake of everything that’s happened. There is not enough food for everyone, and at the same time, the need for food for everyone is much higher because everyone is having to do all of the work to keep civilization going.

It sounds fascinating. To go back to the titular windup girl, how do robots fit into all of this?

Robots are left over from before – there are no labouring robots. The windup girl is a biological construct who was designed as a companion, and she is just loose now, and potentially an object of desire coveted by some of the characters in the book. It’s tied in with this idea of there having been an incredibly opulent, interconnected global society that had things like this, and now she’s a weird relic of a previous time.

Obviously there are still privileged people who have more, but no one on that level. There’s a bit towards the end where there is a revolution, and the government breaks out their fossil fuel reserves – they say, ‘Right, we’re getting the tanks on the streets.’ And no one can really stand against this, but it’s very obvious that they do not have much of this stuff to go. They don’t have many revolutions that they’re going to be able to put down. It is this dreadful situation of a hand about the throat of the people, but even that hand is starving.

Let’s move from robots to a very different extra-human intelligence. Could you tell us about Ray Naylor’s The Mountain in the Sea?

This is interesting. Again, we start with, what is the point of the book? And the point of The Mountain In The Sea is that someone discovers a fully sapient octopus civilization. That aspect is not in any way dystopian. And there is also AI, which is a proper AI. (The standard disambiguation that we science fiction writers now have to give every time we mention AI is: not large language model, spicy-autocorrect nonsense, but actual AI.)

The reason I’m bringing The Mountain and the Sea in as a dystopian novel is the B-plot, which is not the octopuses. It is set on an automated fishing vessel with a crew that are essentially slaves, who have been taken on board this ship and made to do the various menial tasks that it is not worth getting machines to do. The point is what this says about global capitalism in the world that Naylor is writing about… They have an uprising, and they kill the exceedingly oppressive crew of the ship. But they can’t overthrow the ship itself, because the ship itself also has a kind of artificial intelligence. It bottles them up below, and it has various security features that it can kill them with, and it forces them to keep doing the work. It doesn’t care about its killed crew — they turn out to be icing on the cake. So you have a computer enforcing its will on human slave labour – and they’re not convicts or anything, whether that would be a justification or not (I feel probably not). They are just people who’ve been grabbed and shoved on the ship, and that’s going to be the rest of their lives until this ship works them to death. As a microcosm of a capitalism hellscape, it’s astonishing. It’s probably the thing that had the greatest impact on me from that book, even though I love the octopus stuff.

You explore AI in Service Model, your own dystopia. Here, society has collapsed. Our protagonist is a robot, and his sentience is unavoidable because we’re in close-third-person perspective, but his free will is debatable. How would you describe the robot interiority you were setting up here?

This book started because I very much wanted to write from the point of view of a robot. The thing is: what does that actually mean? Because when fiction goes to robots, the temptation is to make them machines that are people, and have thoughts and feelings and desires. They’re basically people in all ways except for their relationship to people-people. You see this right from the beginning – with Frankenstein, I guess, but certainly with Rossum’s Universal Robots and things like that. So as long as we’ve had the word ‘robot’, that’s been what robots were about.

I wanted to think about this. When I’m writing a spider, from a spider’s point of view, I’m not writing a person in a spider suit. I’m trying to make it a spider doing spider things in a way that’s comprehensible to a human reader. In the same way, my character Uncharles is a robot: he doesn’t think in the way that people think, and in fact would claim that he doesn’t really think at all. He has a series of directives. Because he’s a very sophisticated machine, those directives are very sophisticated, and he’s able to improvise a great deal around the idea of trying to fulfil them – up to and including making a whole plan at the end of which is ‘… I will have an owner and be able to do my job again.’ So all of Uncharles’s interiority is based on this idea: if it’s not going to serve his directives queue, then it’s not something he would think of doing.

This means there are things that we would think of as absolutely basic impulses for a human being which Uncharles doesn’t really care about, up to and including self-preservation. There are a variety of circumstances in the book where it’s perfectly logical that he allow himself to be destroyed, because there’s no particular reason why he wouldn’t. As the book goes on, and as things get more complex and confused, he gets more and more inputs – and you start to see that maybe there is more going on with Uncharles’s interior than he would necessarily admit. But it is at least an open question, even at the end of the book, as to just how much Uncharles is a thinking and sapient being, and how much he is simply sentient and following a complex logic chain.

It’s inherently very funny to watch him navigating a distressing dystopian world in his logical way. Were you aiming for a humorous book, or did that emerge once you knew what your robot was like?

I’m a strong believer that if you want to go bleak, you should go funny. This is something I learned weirdly from Joe Abercrombie, who writes incredibly grimdark fiction. He’s one of the best writers of that particular movement, but he’s also very funny with it, which means that his writing is extremely palatable and enjoyable. If it had just been grim, as some of the writers who came after him tried, it would get a bit wearing.

I’ve used this with a number of my books when I’ve been writing about spectacularly horrible things. In this case, it’s the complete collapse of civilization, and all that’s left behind is a bunch of robots who don’t really have a purpose anymore but are still trying to fulfil one.

That could be extremely depressing, but instead, I’ve gone for full-on Douglas Adams-style comedy. That’s somewhat influenced by the fact that one of the big inspirations for the book is a small bit out of the Hitchhiker’s Guide sequence… There’s a world that Zaphod finds himself on where civilization has completely collapsed, and he finds a starship waiting to take off. Inside the ship, people are being kept in suspended animation, and he learns that the ship is awaiting a consignment of lemon-soaked paper napkins before it can take off. So he says, ‘Look, there’s no society out there. Nobody’s making lemon-soaked paper napkins.’ And the ship says quite complacently, ‘At some point a new civilization will arise, and in all probability, it will invent lemon-soaked paper napkins. At that point, we can take off.’ That robotic 100% logic, 100% nonsense position was something I really wanted to explore.

Let’s stay in space and discuss your next choice – you promised us a wacky space opera earlier. Tell us about Hell’s Heart by Alexis Hall.

This is another book which is extremely funny whilst also being extremely bleak. Again, the dystopia stuff is the B-plot. It’s not the main thing: the main thing is a spicy queer retelling of Moby-Dick in space – or depending on your view of Moby-Dick, it’s just a retelling in space, because you can certainly read a lot of that into the original.

So yes: it’s out in space. It is in the far future. Earth is completely abandoned, and people are living in various colonies across the solar system and hunting vast leviathans that live in the upper atmosphere of Jupiter. There is a Captain Ahab, and there is a Queequeg, and there is an Ishmael. But going on behind this is a satirical dystopia.

So how does that factor in?

It’s brought through in the account of the Ishmael character, who is telling you absolutely straight-faced how wonderful everything is: how the rampant exploitative capitalist society they are part of, which requires people to go on these dreadful voyages for a tiny share of the profit, hunting ship-destroying leviathans in terrible environments, is all obviously the way it needs to be. There’s a lot of religion in there, and she belongs to a religious sect, which has a prosperity gospel idea – everyone who is rich is beloved of God. All this is delivered very straight-facedly by the narrator and the writer… The narrator tells you, ‘We were watching this action movie about how, when the amazing defenders of capitalism cracked down on this asteroid miners’ strike, they were right to do so. And those unarmed women and children had it coming’ and so forth… And you can absolutely tell that both the narrator and Hall are shaking the reader and saying, ‘You do see that this is nuts, right?’

Like I say, it’s all just in the background of the whaling stuff. It is a really brutal takedown of a capitalist dystopia, and the ways that capitalism justifies its own predatory ethos.

Hm, I’ve got distracted trying to think of pro-capitalist dystopia takes…

I suspect there were probably plenty back in the day. But yes, overall, I think science fiction tends to skew left rather than right.

We’ve come to your fourth choice, back on Earth: Emma Newman’s After Atlas. Tell us about this one.

This is actually the second book in a series, but they are very independent and can be read individually. In the first book of the series, there was a great big colony ship called Atlas, which, at the behest of a visionary messiah character, goes off to a planet that everyone is assured they can make a colony of. The first book is what happens to that. Then, After Atlas does what those sorts of books generally don’t do, and looks at what happens on Earth.

There’s been an enormous sink of resources into this thing that’s just gone, and an awful lot of the best and brightest have gone with it, and there’s been an immense global depression. In this world, everyone is queuing up for food. Again, it’s an anti-capitalist book, because we may as well look at close-to-home dystopias. There are corporations controlling everything, and they basically use human life as a resource, much like in The Windup Girl.

Who are we following this time?

The main character is someone who has essentially spent their entire childhood on a regimen of drugs and surgery to make them a very specific kind of neurodiverse investigator. The story is about them interacting with a grand conspiracy, and the way that a world which is already in extremely bad shape is going to get massively worse as things go on. I’m not going to spoil some of the reveals in this book. It has one of the most astonishingly gut-punchy moments towards the end that I’ve ever come across in anything I’ve read. But on the way there, we see the mechanisms of control and oppression, up to and including the main character not having control or ownership of their own mind. They’ve been crafted into a tool of the oppressive state from infancy.

Are we meant to be able to solve the mystery they investigate, if we’re paying attention?

From a writer’s point of view, it’s one of those perfect cases where when you find out what’s going on, it’s very obvious that that’s what the book was leading to at all points. But I think you’d have to be a considerably sharper reader than I am to see where it’s going to go – if only because it goes to some spectacularly traumatic places.

Let’s talk about your last book. This is Ian Green’s Extremophile. We’re back where we started with some climate-driven changes… tell us about this one.

Extremophile was nominated for the Arthur C Clarke Award. I was wondering whether to do Gibson’s Neuromancer, because you want some cyberpunk in a dystopia list and one of the problems with a lot of cyberpunk post-Gibson is that there’s lots of cyber but relatively little punk. For me, a genre that wants to have ‘punk’ on the end of its name needs to be against something, in resistance to some sort of systemic issue – so, it should be a perfect ground for writing a dystopia – but a lot of the time, it gets distilled into the fashion and the vibes and the visuals, and you lose that sense of anger and resistance.

Extremophile is biopunk: the technology it looks at is bioengineering rather than traditional cyberware. But it is a book which absolutely brings that angry resistance to the way the world has gone wrong, which in this case is simultaneously corporate and ecological. It’s not a world that has collapsed yet, but it’s a world where a great deal has been lost.

And which part of this world does the book follow?

It’s a book about angry young people who are living in an underclass in a broken state, where all of the power is concentrated in a vanishingly small set of hands. They’re doing what they can to fight back against the man. We started with the question: why do we read dystopia? Bizarrely enough, 1984 aside, dystopian narratives are frequently wildly optimistic, because you do get to fight back against the man – whether it’s Gibson or The Hunger Games or Extremophile. In most of these stories, there is some sort of blow that the ordinary person can inflict against the brutal and oppressive world that they find themselves in. That is maybe the real reason we like dystopias: because they tend to still have hope. Most of us, when we write dystopias, go towards an ending where something has been achieved. That gives a satisfying narrative payout for the reader: that even though the world is dreadful, we can still do something.

Would you say your choices today are optimistic about human nature?

They all recognise the complexity of human nature. None of them take the position that everyone is bad and it’s all Lord of the Flies out there. I prefer to read books about complicated people and complicated societies.

entries.title: The Best Body Horror Books, recommended by Heather Parry
entries.summary: Body horror is often bloody and gory, argues the novelist Heather Parry, but it is also a vessel for social commentary. Here she recommends five books that explore notions of bodily autonomy, capitalism and technology through the form of a horror novel – cult hits that will make you wince, but also make you think. This interview appeared first on Five Books.
entries.content:
What does ‘body horror’ mean to you, and what makes for a good body horror book?

For me, body horror is fiction about the violation of, or transformation of, the human body – at the hands of ourselves, another, or an entity, such as the state or technology. It tends towards dense descriptions of bodily violations, which is why it’s so often thought of as ‘gory’, but it doesn’t necessarily have to, because even the suggestion of the transformation or violation is enough to shock and affect us, as readers.

For me the visceral element is less important than the social commentary, which I think is inherent in the genre. If it isn’t in some way critical or political, then it really is just gore, in my mind. I don’t even think works of body horror have to be strictly within the genre of horror, but I do think there has to be a level of social critique within it; for instance, I think there’s a case to be made that James Kelman’s Booker Prize-winning How Late It Was, How Late could be categorised as body horror, as it follows a man who has been made blind through police violence, and then is trapped in a Kafkaesque world of bureaucracy because of not only his blindness but his class position. It is about the multiple violences visited on a person by the neglectful or oppressive state, and the body is used as a metaphor within this.

But I think, for most people, the genre has to sit within horror more clearly, and has to contain some sort of extreme physicality. A really good body horror book, for me, manages to make salient political or social points whilst using visceral description that evokes both sympathy and disgust; that is where the really great work is.

That’s an interesting way to frame it. Your first book recommendation is Geek Love by Katharine Dunn, which was published in 1989. It’s about purposeful mutation during pregnancy, and the premise is pretty horrifying. Could you introduce us to it?

It’s a truly mad, brilliant novel. Al Binewski, the owner of a travelling carnival, marries a Boston aristocrat who has run away from privilege to become an aerialist, but suffers a catastrophic injury that curtails her planned career. Needing to drum up interest in the carnival, they decide to have children and to expose Lil to prescription drugs, insecticides and ‘radioisotopes’ in order to intentionally mutate their children, so they can perform in the carnival and always have something unique that they can monetise; an ‘inherited security’ of the type Lil’s privileged background gave her.

The children who result from this experiment are Arturo, who has flippers instead of arms or legs; the beautiful conjoined twins Electra and Iphigenia; our narrator Olympia, who has albinism, dwarfism and a hunchback; and Fortunato, who is telekinetic. From this wild premise Katharine Dunn spins a book that is about many different things – bodies and capitalism, cultism, how love becomes bad, chosen family, incest, faulty feminism, and the curse of being ‘normal’.

But the violation of the physical is the key to all of this; the cult that rises up around Arturo involves followers increasingly cutting off parts of their bodies in order to move closer towards what they call ‘PIP’: peace, isolation and purity. I don’t think it’s a coincidence that Katharine Dunn, who managed to draw all this out of a book about body horror, also wrote extensively on boxing.

Despite its dark concept, the book continues to sell and is credited as inspiring work by anyone from Kurt Cobain and Courtney Love to Terry Gilliam. Why do you think it has such a hold on people?

I can’t speak for everyone but for me, it totally blew open what I thought a novel could be, which is perhaps why it has inspired so many creative people. It is simply rammed with ideas and refuses to tell you what to think about any of it. It is absolutely unconcerned with the idea that its central conceit might offend or disgust; you can sort of imagine the eviscerating social media reviews it would get now for its portrayal of two parents willingly subjecting their own pregnancies to toxic materials in order to make their kids ‘special’.

The idea of a parent – especially a mother – making actively malign choices on behalf of her children is still taboo, but because it is so taboo it is very effective in getting us to think about structural violence, absolute power, and physical vulnerability to those who are supposed to care for us, which is an enduring and inescapable horror; it is for all these reasons that I was drawn to this topic in my second novel Carrion Crow as well.

If this, supposedly the purest love that exists, can be soured, used against us and made violent, then there is nothing on which we can truly rely. It forces us to question everything. In the age of social media and ‘mommy bloggers’ who destroy their children’s lives by forcing them to be unpaid performers the minute they are born, this book takes on an entirely contemporary meaning too: how does money and fame corrupt family relationships in the age of the constant camera? It could be notorious ‘mommy blogger’ Ruby Franke rather than Lil Binewski who says: ‘What greater gift could you offer your children than an inherent ability to earn a living just by being themselves?’

Next you’ve selected J.G. Ballard’s The Atrocity Exhibition, an experimental 1970 book of what the author called “condensed fictions.” Can you tell us more, and why you recommend it?

The Atrocity Exhibition was Ballard’s first book after he lost his wife Mary; they went on holiday with their three young children, and she caught pneumonia and was dead within days. He returned to England a widower at 33 and a single parent to three kids under ten, who he was advised to give away to other family members, as it wasn’t seen as ‘correct’ for a man to be raising children alone.

The Atrocity Exhibition was essentially his response to this completely brutal series of events, and marked a huge shift away from his previous sci-fi novels and towards a much more avant-garde approach to the technological age that was unfolding around him. In it he manages to connect his own grief to very public displays of violence, such as the Kennedy assassination and the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, as well as the landscape created by the media, the automobile, television, and celebrity culture within the 1960s.

The result is a borderline unreadable and completely fragmented collection of stories connected mostly by theme, structure and the fact that all contain a self-insert character who goes by different versions of the same name – Travers, Talbert, Travis, et cetera – with names like ‘Notes Towards a Mental Breakdown’ and ‘Why I Want to Fuck Ronald Reagan.’

My next book, which will be out in February 2027, is hugely inspired by The Atrocity Exhibition, but Ballard’s is a book so of its time that it is impossible to write a version of it today; the things he writes about – celebrity culture, politics and the media – have now combined so successfully as to be completely unmappable onto his model of society. It’s a book that is unique in every way, and unrepeatable, and hugely inspiring because of that. It reminds me to be weirder, be bolder, and to break apart everything that’s deemed acceptable in fiction.

I find J. G. Ballard’s writing so haunting, so unnerving. I hadn’t really thought of him as writing body horror, specifically, but yes, of course it is. What parts of this book do you respond to most?

For me The Atrocity Exhibition is indisputably body horror because it is about the intersection of the technological and the human, and it maps in its own unhinged style how the technological age violates both the mind and the body. The loose ‘plot’ of the book is that of a psychiatrist in charge of a psychiatric facility, who himself undergoes a breakdown and loses himself to psychosis; in trying to make sense of all these real-world events he plays them over and over, and within these fragmented imaginings the human body is brutalised. Marilyn Monroe becomes the victim of a nuclear bomb. Ronald Reagan’s is transposed onto the bodies of collision victims for sexual purposes. Mae west undergoes a breast reduction.

Ballard himself studied for a medical degree before he dropped out to become a writer, and he used to have a doctor friend send him the contents of his waste paper bin so he could go through medical reports and studies, so the body is totally abject here. The car crash is a recurring theme, as his next novel Crash is present here as a short story, and we see the ways that he seeds the sexualisation of violence throughout the book; the mechanically-degraded physique is hugely fetishised by other humans. In so many ways this is a book about violence and what it does to the human body, but also our collective psyche and our social structures. It is this that I am so interested in.

Next you’ve selected Beloved by Toni Morrison. Earlier you said this would be “a controversial choice” but you had solid logic to back it up. Tell me more!

Beloved is the story of a formerly enslaved woman, Sethe, who lives a cloistered existence with her 18 year old daughter Denver in a house haunted by the ghost of her first child. With the arrival of Paul D, who was enslaved on the same plantation as Sethe, mother and daughter are brought once again into society, but the ghost is driven out of the home; when they return one day they find a girl, Beloved, on the front porch of the house. Both Denver and eventually Sethe come to believe that Beloved is Sethe’s first child returned to them, and her presence in the home reveals brutal family secrets and the long effects of absolute trauma.

When I studied Beloved at university it was on an American fiction course and we were introduced to it as a type of Southern Gothic, but I think it is more than this. I think many people would balk at the idea of this being a body horror book, but it is, for me, about the ultimate physical violation: slavery, the turning of a person into a commodity. It is the inescapable fact from which all the individual stories in the novel are wrought.

From this central violation it touches on many others: the rape of both male and female enslaved people, maternal filicide, the uneven landscape of suffering, pregnancy as an instrument of female oppression even outside of the plantation. It is horror of the most physical type. Like all the most affecting, enduring horror it takes its inspiration from a real case, that of Margaret Garner, that exposes the greatest crimes of humanity and what they do to a person.

As the Guardian noted in a review of your own Carrion Crow, “you don’t tend to encounter much body horror in historical fiction.” Would you talk a little about your decision to bring these two elements together—transgression or taboo with the mannerliness we tend to project upon the past?

There definitely have been other novels that bring the two together – I’m thinking of Ottessa Moshfegh’s Lapvona, and Eat Him If You Like by Jean Teulé – but in Carrion Crow I was very much inspired by Mrs Beeton’s Book of Household Management, a real Victorian domestic guide that basically hasn’t been out of print since it was published in 1861.

My mother had a copy of this very archaic looking book when I was growing up but never referred to it; when I got my own kitchen in my thirties I bought an old copy and really got lost in its descriptions of foods, of how to butcher and prepare things, but also in its advice around motherhood and child-rearing.

At one point, Isabella Beeton refers to a nursing child as a ‘baby vampire’, and it was this strikingly modern, strikingly horror-inflected phrase that got me thinking about the physical horrors of the Victorian era – not just in terms of the oppression of women but with regards to the machinations of the British Empire, which was bringing all this blossoming wealth to the country as a result of colonisation-induced famines and the forced labour in service of industry.

In the novel the latter is kept peripheral, explored through the growing influence of a soap magnate based on Lord Leverhulme (whose soap empire became Unilever, and whose wealth was inextricably linked to the horrifying treatment of workers in Belgian-controlled Congo, which reduced the Congolese population by half) but the former is made manifest in the physical degradation of Marguerite, the protagonist, at the hands of her mother, Cécile.

For me, body horror seemed the most natural and most effective way to make readers consider these things, and in doing so, to consider the foundations of the society we live in today.

That brings us to Rosemary’s Baby, the 1967 novel by Ira Levin. I think a lot of our readers will be familiar with the Roman Polanski movie that was released the following year, with Mia Farrow in the lead role. But the original book is worth revisiting?

Absolutely it is; Levin’s books do not waste any time. This and The Stepford Wives make for a great weekend double bill. I’m sure everyone knows the story here, and the sort of hysterical premise, but when you strip away the fantastical and religious elements it is really a book about being betrayed, in the worst, most physical and psychological way, by the person you are supposed to be able to trust – and by the entire community around you. It is about the whole world falling away from you: not only your partner, but the doctors and neighbours who are supposed to be your saviours. This is handled in such a way to make you really question Rosemary throughout, to not know what is real, and in that way you, the reader, become a function of this systemic violence against this woman. It could be called Gaslighting: The Novel.

Levin really makes pregnancy seem completely alien, a desecrating process, and then if you read the story as an allegory he even touches on postpartum psychosis. There truly are women who have believed their newborns to be the devil, with catastrophic consequences. It is just a book you can come back to again and again and get something new from it. There is something I absolutely adore about 1960s and 1970s horror novels too, and it’s that they remember they are supposed to be mass market entertainment, eventually becoming paperbacks that would be shoved into someone’s jeans pocket: they move like steam trains, totally impossible to put down. Levin really does not waste a word. But having said that, the film is also one of my all-time favourites, so do both.

It’s interesting that you have two books on the list exploring horrifying pregnancies. Is gestation the ur-body horror?

I think it is, because it is in many ways completely unknowable as a personal process – until you’re in the midst of it, then the only way out is through – and yet it is one we largely, now, throw ourselves into. I think it’s a layered body horror in that way: it’s a violation of your body as your own, as a thing you know intimately, as a thing you have total control over, but it’s also a violation that you invite, if you are lucky enough not to have been impregnated against your will.

In pregnancy you’re made vulnerable not only to the outside world and all its many and various threats, but to the medical system, and even to the man who you’re having this child with, if you’re in a heterosexual relationship; it carries with it an inescapable critique of all these systems of power. This is quite the combination of things to reckon with, and then you’ve got the corporeal reality of it: the daily transformation, the medical risks, the fact that you spontaneously grow a brand new organ which you’ll then birth out. All new, all beautiful, all potentially dangerous, all completely outwith your control. And under all that is the parental terror, of course: the ultimate responsibility to this new, vulnerable person inside you, the constant tension between their needs and yours, the abject and all consuming fear that you can do all the ‘right’ things, do your unequivocal best for them, and something still might happen to take them away.

Then of course, even if all goes well, and by some divine luck both parent and child are well, you are irreversibly changed, physically and mentally, forever. It is a miracle that we go through it so casually, really.

Finally, we’ve come to Under the Skin by Michel Faber, which was a huge discovery for me as a teenager. It’s such a strange and invigorating book. Would you introduce it to our readers?

Invigorating is the right word – and it’s wild to think this was his debut. It follows Isserley, an alien living in human form, as she drives up and down the A9 road in Scotland picking up male hitchhikers. Eventually we learn that she is actually harvesting these men so that they can be fattened up and slaughtered by her colleagues, and sent back to her home planet as a highly-prized meat, primarily eaten by the elite who live above ground. Everyone else is forced to labour underground.

It is such a brilliant concept as the very case of being a human being is othered; Isserley has been subjected to deforming surgeries to make her look human, leaving her in pain and alienated from her own body. And then the actual humans are othered; Isserley is sexually assaulted by one of them and consents to watching him be processed, which means he is castrated and has his tongue cut out before he is slaughtered; she is both horrified and disappointed by this process. But she intensely identifies with the sheep, and increasingly with her prey; it is a book that uses body horror to explore what it actually means to be an animal amongst other animals. And then, of course, there’s the critique of the meat industry too; Under the Skin walked so Tender is the Flesh could run.

This book has been adapted for the screen too, with Scarlett Johansson in the lead role. It is quite different to the book. Do you have a preference?

I think they’re entirely complementary. Jonathan Glazer’s film is not really telling the narrative of the novel; I really think of it as an artistic response to the book rather than a straight adaptation of it – a really bold and interesting choice which I wish we had more of! It’s one of those rare versions of a book that really leans into the possibilities of cinema, and putting Scarlett Johansson, the Hollywood film star, into direct interaction with regular Scottish people to evoke the idea of alienness is just inspired. It really deals with the body horror of the novel gorgeously too; the dropping of the men into the sort of black liquid instantly others the body, and the scene where Isserley strips off her human skin reminds me so much of the controversial Anatomy for Beginners series that Gunter von Hagens did for Channel 4 in 2005. There was one episode where he ‘degloved’ a cadaver (it means exactly what you think) which imprinted itself on my 19 year old brain, and the way she strips her arms is identical, in my mind, to the way the fat and sinew was revealed beneath human flesh. Then when she looks at her own blinking face: that is the definition of the uncanny, the unheimlich. Brilliant. I think you can approach the combination in either direction – read the book then watch the movie, or vice versa – but you should definitely do both.

Finally: what is it, do you think, that so attracts you to this mode of writing – body horror?

I think it is how successful it is in making the political personal, and how broad the scope of it really is. I recently ran a body horror workshop at the Alasdair Gray Archive and the Agnes Owens Archive, where I’ve been doing a part time residency for the last six months, and it is amazing to see how quickly people take to the genre even when they think they have no interest in it. We looked at Gray’s Poor Things and the Owens short story Arabella and talked about how they used body horror to explore social themes and power structures, then I invited them to bring in their own experiences of violation or transformation, and all of a sudden there opens up a huge landscape on which to write. The stories they created even within a short class were varied, impactful, funny, grim, gross, politically astute and totally unique. For me, the very best literature challenges power even in a small way, forces readers to think about the ways in which society has grown rotten, and in doing both inspires us towards creative change, resistance and empathy. I think body horror is such a strong tool for achieving this—while giving us books that are entertaining, impactful and unforgettable.
